newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Italy's new car sales see April record rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Italy's new car sales see April record rise.

text.p: Italy's new car market showed a record rise in April as the nation's new car buying incentive scheme encouraged more and more purchasers into car show rooms after four years of sluggish demand.

Italy's Ministry of Transport figures on Friday showed that April new registrations rocketed 52.37 percent higher to 231,500 compared to April 1996, and set the Italian market on course to top two million cars this year for the first time since 1992.

The nation's dominant car maker Fiat responded to the boost from the scheme and managed to increase its market share in April to 44.90 percent, up from 44.35 percent in April 1996 and also ahead of 43.55 percent in March 1997.
"This is a phenomenal figure for April and shows the effects of the incentive scheme," said analyst Bob Barber at HSBC James Capel as the figure came around 10 percent above his forecast.
This April rise comes after an increase seen in March of 25.04 percent and a 21.45 percent rise in February.

Italy introduced its new car incentive scheme, funded by the government and industry, in January to run until the end of September in which car owners receive price discounts on new cars when they trade in cars more than 10 years old.
Most analysts and industry bodies are predicting the new car market will rise above two million in 1997, the highest since 1992 when sales reached 2.389 million and above 1996's 1.737 million.
Analysts say Fiat is forecasting a 20 percent rise in sales for the Italian market in 1997, totally due to the incentive scheme, in a market Fiat sees reaching 2.08 million units.

The large April rise in Italy helped western European new car sales increase 9.2 percent to 1,258,200 in April, but without Italy the rise would only have been 2.6 percnet, said Italian vehicle makers association Anfia.

In the first four months of 1997, European new car sale rose 0.6 percent, but without Italy there would have been a 3.6 percent fall. In April, new car sales rose 1.3 percent in Germany, Britain was up 11.8 percent and Spain up 19.2 percent, while the fall in French sales continued, down 10 percent.

Fiat, which also takes in Alfa Romeo and Lancia, saw its own new car sales in April rise 23.3 percent with the group's European market share rising to 12.7 percent in April from 11.2 percent in April 1996 maintaining the group in second place in the European car market after German carmaker Volkswagen.

But many commentators were turning to concerns over what happens when the incentive scheme ends. Italy's car importers' association Unrae said revisions to administrative and fiscal laws were need to make buying cars easier and cheaper.

Some looked at the situation in France where a car incentive scheme ended last year and the market then declined. Analysts say the longer an incentive scheme runs the bigger will be the decline in the market at the end of the scheme.

Fiat, which had struggled to meet the increase in demand for new cars in the first quarter of 1997, is now beginning to see the financial benefits of the scheme after its operating margins started to show a clear improvement in March.
Fiat said earlier this week that its operating margin across all its industrial operations reached 4.4 percent in March after averaging 2.6 percent during the first quarter of 1997.
